issues.subject: Research Room: diary studies that people finish
issues.text:
THE RESEARCH ROOM
Notes on UX research. {weekday} {date}

View in your browser: https://researchroom.example/notes/research-room-diary-studies-that-people-finish

Hello, researchers. This week: how to keep diary study participants going past day four, a recruiting tip for hard-to-reach professionals, and three new jobs. Applications for our November workshop on synthesis close on Friday 30 October.

METHOD

Diary studies that people finish
Most diary studies lose a third of their participants by the end of the first week. Hedda ran two this summer and tried three changes: one prompt a day instead of three, a short call on day two to answer questions, and paying a small amount after each entry rather than all at the end. Completion went from 58% to 91%. The per-entry payment did most of the work.

RECRUITING

Finding pharmacists, nurses and other shift workers
Offer sessions at 7am and 9pm, not just in office hours, and say so in the screener's first line. We doubled our response rate from hospital staff this way.

WORTH READING

Synthesis on a wall versus in a tool
A team compares a week of sticky notes with a week in a whiteboard app. The wall won, narrowly, for reasons that have nothing to do with the tool.

Read: https://researchroom.example/go/synthesis-on-a-wall-versus-in-a-tool

issues.subject: Research Room: the five-second test, revisited
issues.text:
THE RESEARCH ROOM
Notes on UX research. {weekday} {date}

View in your browser: https://researchroom.example/notes/research-room-the-five-second-test-revisited

Hello, researchers. One method we'd written off, one reading that changed our minds about incentives, and the usual jobs.

METHOD

The five-second test, revisited
Sam had dismissed five-second tests as a gimmick until a client used them to settle a long argument about a homepage. Show the page for five seconds, hide it, and ask one question: what does this company do? Thirty participants, one afternoon, and the answer was clear. It won't tell you why, but it ends a certain kind of meeting quickly.

RECRUITING

Screeners that don't give the game away
If your screener asks 'Do you use budgeting apps?' first, everyone says yes. Ask about money habits in general and put the app question fourth, among others.

WORTH READING

What incentives buy you, and what they don't
A long look at how payment amounts change who turns up, with numbers from 400 studies.

Read: https://researchroom.example/go/what-incentives-buy-you-and-what-they-don-t

issues.subject: Research Room: interviewing in a second language
issues.text:
THE RESEARCH ROOM
Notes on UX research. {weekday} {date}

View in your browser: https://researchroom.example/notes/research-room-interviewing-in-a-second-language

Hello, researchers. This issue is about language: running sessions in a language that isn't yours, and when to bring in an interpreter instead.

METHOD

Interviewing in a second language
Hedda runs about a third of her sessions in Swedish, which she speaks well but not natively. Her advice: write the guide in the participant's language, not a translation of your English one; leave longer silences than feels natural; and record everything, because you will miss things. When the topic is sensitive, use an interpreter you've briefed, even if you're fluent.

RECRUITING

Pay participants in the way they prefer
Vouchers suit some people, bank transfers others, and a few would rather you donate to a charity. Asking in the screener costs one question and earns a lot of goodwill.

WORTH READING

A glossary of research terms in six languages
Built by a multilingual team in Brussels. Useful for writing consent forms.

Read: https://researchroom.example/go/a-glossary-of-research-terms-in-six-languages

issues.subject: Research Room: say what you didn't find
issues.text:
THE RESEARCH ROOM
Notes on UX research. {weekday} {date}

View in your browser: https://researchroom.example/notes/research-room-say-what-you-didn-t-find

Hello, researchers. This week's method note is about reports, and one paragraph we think every report should have.

METHOD

Say what you didn't find
Every study goes in with questions it can't answer. Most reports quietly drop them. We now end each report with a short section called 'What this study can't tell you', listing the questions we couldn't answer and why: too few participants of a certain kind, a prototype that didn't cover the flow, a topic people wouldn't talk about. Stakeholders read it more closely than anything else in the report.

RECRUITING

Over-recruit by 20%, always
No-show rates in our studies this year averaged 14% for remote sessions and 22% in person. Book extras and pay them if they're not needed.

WORTH READING

Research repositories nobody opens
An honest write-up from a team that built one, and the three changes that got people using it.

Read: https://researchroom.example/go/research-repositories-nobody-opens

issues.subject: Research Room: guerrilla testing done properly
issues.text:
THE RESEARCH ROOM
Notes on UX research. {weekday} {date}

View in your browser: https://researchroom.example/notes/research-room-guerrilla-testing-done-properly

Hello, researchers. A defence of testing in cafes and libraries, with the rules we follow so that it's still research.

METHOD

Guerrilla testing done properly
Quick, informal testing in public places gets a bad name because it's often done badly. Our rules: decide in advance who you need and walk away from anyone who isn't them; use a consent card even for ten minutes; keep the task to one flow; and write notes straight after each person, not at the end of the day. Done this way, an afternoon in a library gave a client more than a month of surveys.

RECRUITING

Ask the venue first
Libraries are usually happy to help if you ask the manager a week ahead. Some will put up a sign.

WORTH READING

The ethics of testing with strangers
A short, practical piece on consent and data when your participants are passers-by.

Read: https://researchroom.example/go/the-ethics-of-testing-with-strangers

issues.subject: Research Room: card sorting with 200 cards
issues.text:
THE RESEARCH ROOM
Notes on UX research. {weekday} {date}

View in your browser: https://researchroom.example/notes/research-room-card-sorting-with-200-cards

Hello, researchers. This issue is for anyone facing a website with far too many pages. We have opinions about card sorting at scale.

METHOD

Card sorting with 200 cards
Nobody can sort 200 cards well. We split them into overlapping sets of 50, with ten cards common to every set so we can compare groups. Each participant sorts one set. With 15 participants per set we get stable groups, and the shared cards tell us whether the sets agree. Write the cards in your users' words, not your sitemap's, or you're testing your own labels.

RECRUITING

Unmoderated is fine for sorting
Card sorts work well unmoderated. Save your moderated hours for tree tests, where you'll want to ask why people went the wrong way.

WORTH READING

Information architecture for museums
A case study on organising 3,000 collection pages, with the card sort results.

Read: https://researchroom.example/go/information-architecture-for-museums
